full_judgment: 8. I have gone through the judgments of both the courts below and also Exhibits as filed by both the parties. Admitted fact is that the CS Khatian was prepared in the name of Jagadish and Ashutosh from where the plaintiff claims the ownership but the pattans were not produced by plaintiff and defendant before the court though RS was prepared in the name of the predecessor of the plaintiff and defendants. The plaintiff produced some dakhilas and also rent receipts i.e. Exhibit 5 which appeared to have been paid on 16-3-1980 and Exhibit 5 Ka is paid in 1969 in the name of Tayab Khan and Exhibit 6 series are the dakhilas given by the jaminder and the defendants have also filed rent receipts of the government which were marked as Exhibit A series and admitted position is that he paid rent up to 1991. The defendants have mutated and submitted some documents of that purchase deed of different dates i.e. 12-3-1979 and 5-12-1979. The dakhilas submitted by the plaintiff are the private documents and that are ie, to be proved by the scribe, the signatures are to be compared which were not considered by the lower appellate Court. These private dakhilas are yet to be proved and it is referred in 35 DLR 129 "that dakhilas are private documents and it would not carry any presumption of correctness as would be available in the case of any entry in the record of rights under the provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act. It appears that both the parties have adduced rent receipts and the petitioner has paid rent up to 1991 and there was mutation though the mutation proceeding is under challenge in the appeal and, according to decision 35 DLR (AD) 216, rent receipts are evidence of possession, and may be used as collateral evidence of title. The petitioner has submitted certain rent receipts marked as Exhibit A series which were not considered by the learned appellate Court. Though it is a question of fact based on finding and is proved and this aspect since not discussed by the learned appellate Court, I find substance in this Rule. Since rent receipts are evidence of possession and collateral evidence of title and in a suit for permanent injunction where the plaintiff did not mention the boundary of the specific plot and there is no specific demarcation, in that view of the matter, granting injunction in favour of the plaintiff cannot be sustained.
